Honorer la tradition et la souveraineté: Honouring Tradition and Sovereignty: Some Vote, Many Don’t in Kanehsatà:ke
Kanehsatà:ke est reconnue pour faire pre: Kanehsatà:ke is known for its political resistance.
Cet article fait suite à celui que j'ai: This article follows the one I wrote about electoral abstention among residents of Kahnwà:ke. The Mohawks of Kanehsatà:ke share the same attitude toward voting as their Kanien'kehá:ka neighbours 60 kilometres away.
Cet article présente une génération plus: This article features an older generation. Besides the people interviewed below, other members of the Kahnesatà:ke community I spoke with anonymously told me they don’t vote because they feel it is a pointless act that would cost them their status as members of the nation. I want to take more time to meet and interview people so that other voices can be heard in my upcoming articles on Kanien'kéha:ka issues.
Kanehsatà:ke, une communauté kanien'kehá: Kanehsatà:ke, a Kanien'kehá:ka (Mohawk) community on the shore of the Lake of Two Mountains, 50 km west of Montréal, is known for its political resistance.
Un grand nombre de Québécois connaissent: Many Quebecers know Kanehsatà:ke because of the Kanesatake resistance – better known as the Oka Crisis – in which, in 1990, community members opposed the expansion of a golf course onto their unceded territory, which included a cemetery. After a 78-day standoff between Kanien'kehá:ka land defenders, Quebec police, the RCMP and the Canadian army, the golf course expansion was cancelled, but the land was not returned to the community: <l1>it was purchased by the federal government</l1>. <l2>To this day, ownership of the land is still disputed</l2> between the neighbouring town of Oka, Kanehsatà:ke and the federal government.
À l'heure actuelle, cette communauté con: Today, the community remains politically engaged; <l1>band council elections are still very lively</l1>. But, <l2>like their fellow Mohawks in Kahnawà:ke</l2>, many of them do not vote in Canadian federal elections. The people of Kanehsatà:ke make up about 2,750 of the <l3>100,600 residents of Mirabel, their electoral riding</l3>.
<strong>« Nous ne participons pas au vot: “We don’t take part in white society’s vote”
L’aîné, Gordie Oke, suit de près la poli: Elder Gordie Oke closely follows Canadian and American politics. However, he will not vote in the federal election. “As Mohawk people, we don’t take part in white society’s vote, because it has not kept its promises throughout history,” he explains.
S'adressant aux Canadiens non autochtone: Speaking to non-Indigenous Canadians who want to know why Mohawks don’t vote, Gordie Oke says: “We are different from you, but we are part of society. Don’t forget that you are the invaders of our land, and that governments, religion, the courts have always wronged us. So I don’t want to take part in that.”
Selon lui, les promesses politiques futu: He says future political promises, such as the return of land, or possible political threats to Indigenous rights, don’t push him to go vote. “Their words are just words.... Governments only have words on their lips. [They say] a program will be set up, it will cost $20 million, but it will be spread over ten years. Then the next government comes in and can change everything. There’s no hope. Maybe one day there will be. But for now, it’s pretty hard,” says Gordie Oke.
L'aîné ne méprise pas les Mohawks qui ch: The elder doesn’t look down on Mohawks who choose to vote, but it’s not something he plans to do anytime soon. “Not many Mohawks on Turtle Island vote. Some do. That’s fine. It’s an individual choice and I believe in that. Exercise your rights if you want to. But for many of us, we’d rather not. It’s as simple as that.”
<strong>« Le gouvernement fédéral est le: “The federal government is the trustee and we are the beneficiaries”
Serge Simon, chef du <l1>Conseil Mohawk: Serge Simon, Grand Chief of the <l1>Mohawk Council of Kanesatake</l1>, voted in the last federal election. “In our case, because of our treaties, the British Crown is the guarantor, the federal government is the trustee and we are the beneficiaries of that trust. Of course, in any trust, I have a say in who will administer my benefits. That’s as far as I go by voting in the election,” he says.
Il respecte, dit-il, l'opinion des gens: He says he respects the opinion of people who don’t vote, but thinks it is important to see the link between the federal government and what happens on the territory. He is considering voting in this election after seeing that the federal government can both harm and help his community. Provincial and federal neglect, along with a handful of Kanehsatà:ke residents, <l1>left the lands of Kanehsatà:ke contaminated by the illegal dumping of toxic substances at a “recycling centre” (G&R Recycling) for nearly a decade</l1>.
Bien que de nombreux habitants de Kanehs: Although many Kanehsatà:ke residents sounded the alarm, the provincial government only revoked the dump’s operating permit after<l1> a 2020 investigation by The Rover, Ricochet Media and The Eastern Door</l1>. The federal government gave the community $3.5 million to reclaim the land, and a provincial injunction <l2>put an end to the illegal dumping</l2>.
« Il faut que les gens comprennent que c: “People need to understand that what happens in Kanehsatà:ke, whether it’s organized crime, dumping or any other problem, is directly linked to the federal government’s negligence,” adds Serge Simon. “If we had had the necessary resources, this wouldn’t have happened or would have been minimized very quickly. That’s the will of the Crown, not the Council’s or anyone else’s. People like to point the finger at the Council, but really, it’s like blaming a diabetic for their diabetes,” he says.
Serge Simon envisage de voter lors de ce: Serge Simon is considering voting in this election to keep a Conservative government out. In 2012, Stephen Harper’s Conservative government weakened <l1>the environmental protection act and the environmental assessment act</l1>. He fears that Pierre Poilievre will <l2>continue dismantling federal environmental protections </l2>and <l3>increase oil and gas production</l3>.
« Ces gars-là ne pensent qu’au pétrole e: “These guys only think about oil and gas. They clearly work for the energy industry. They don’t really care about the rest. They pretend to, but I don’t trust Poilievre. He’s just another version of Harper, maybe even worse. The environment needs to be protected. The Conservatives are certainly not the party for that,” he says.
<strong>« Nous nous éloignerions de notr: “We would be moving away from our own nation”
Katsi'tén:hawe Linda David Cree. Photo :: Katsi'tén:hawe Linda David Cree. Photo: Spencer Turcotte
Katsi'tén:hawe Linda David Cree, voit le: Katsi'tén:hawe Linda David Cree sees things differently. Katsi'tén:hawe is curriculum coordinator for the Mohawk Language Custodian Association, a non-profit organization whose mandate is to revitalize the Kanien'kéha (Mohawk) culture and language.
« Cela remonte à loin : mes parents et m: “It goes back a long way: my parents and my grandparents didn’t vote. Being traditional, raised in the tradition, we believe we would be moving away from our own nation [by voting], and that being in favour of sovereignty [voting] would keep me from being who I am, which is Haudenosaunee, the Six Nations Confederacy,” she explains.
« Certains disent que si l'on a une cart: “Some say that if you have a Canadian status card, that makes us Canadian.
Mais je ne vois pas les choses de cette: But I don’t see it that way, because in a way, you’re forced to acknowledge it in order to benefit from the services available to everyone,” she continues.
Les idées politiques de Katsi'tén:hawe v: Katsi'tén:hawe’s political ideas also aim to revive the traditional Mohawk way of life, namely the longhouse government, where leaders are chosen by clan mothers.
« C'est aux mères de clan de s'assurer q: “It’s up to the clan mothers to make sure their choices [of representatives] are good ones. They’re supposed to watch the young people as they grow up. You need skilled speakers, a big heart, a good mind and great kindness. You want the best to be the spokesperson for their community,” she explains.
Dans le même ordre d'idées, Katsi'tén:ha: Along the same lines, Katsi'tén:hawe doesn’t vote in band council elections either. “It’s an arm of the federal government. It was imposed in the 1880s. We didn’t ask for it. It was imposed on us. They even killed <l1>a chief from Akwesasne </l1>[Jake Ice-Saiowisakeron] to set up the electoral system. That system was imposed to get rid of the traditional chiefs.”
La fidélité de Katsi'tén:hawe à la tradi: Katsi'tén:hawe’s loyalty to tradition has brought her some hurdles: she refuses, for instance, to get a passport. Still, she wouldn’t want it any other way. “I’ve really tried all my life, with my husband, to follow this very strict path. We were married in the longhouse with our chiefs from the three communities. We named our children in the longhouse,” she says.
Elle le répète : « J'aime la position qu: She says it again: “I like the position I’ve taken throughout my life. I honour my parents for that. And I wouldn’t choose another life, even though it’s been very hard.”
